title: Cultivating A Culture
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino uses the story of turning a bare, mossy garden into a shared neighbourhood effort as an extended analogy for building school culture. Her point is that real culture change is slow, deep and consistent, not a matter of posters and assemblies. Saying we are respectful is like planting bright flowers without working the soil, whereas culture is built when respect shows up in every interaction from asking for help to queueing in the dining hall. She lists seven steps, starting small, explaining principles, modelling every time, praising, ensuring consistency and diagnosing inconsistency. She notes that these are the same steps used to build classroom culture, only scaled up to more people.
points: Visible slogans and assemblies are superficial; culture changes only when principles run through everyday interactions at every level.
Teachers and leaders must model desired behaviours every single time, since good behaviour from some spreads to others only in a supportive culture.
Whole-school culture uses the same steps as classroom routines, so it can be grown outward from classrooms.
Investigating why behaviour is inconsistent, and supporting everyone to a consistent level, is a necessary step.
quotes: Change did not happen immediately- we worked hard at it, made deep changes rather than suferficial ones and now, every year, we take great care in maintaining, refining, and working some more on our garden.

A great school culture encourages all students to flourish. Just like with the work on the gardens, good, attentive learning behaviours displayed by some individuals can spur similar behaviours in others, provided the right culture exists. It is our job, as teachers and leaders, to cultivate this culture and maintain it consistently.
The only way school culture can be successful is if all members of the community value the principles guiding it. These principles need to be threaded through everything that happens at every level.

For example, it is easy to say that ‘We are respectful’ in our school, put this on posters everywhere and say it in assemblies once a half-term. These are superficial changes. Very visible changes, like planting new, bright flowers but not doing anything with the soil.
Sound familiar? These are the steps we take to build a successful classroom culture and good routines. The only difference is it is scaled-up and involves a lot more people.

We started small when we worked on our garden and now we discuss improvements and maintenance with others on our street. In the same way, we can start with cultivating the right culture in classrooms and build it up so it permeates everything within a school.
